output.title: Why does ice float in my drink?
output.summary: Ice floats because freezing spreads water out, making ice less dense than liquid water.
learningObjectives: Explain that ice floats because ice is less dense than liquid water
Explain that ice spreads out when it freezes
misconceptionNotes: Floating is not only about being heavy or light. A big heavy ice cube can float while a tiny heavy rock sinks, because what matters is density for the same size.

steps.title: Ice in your glass
steps.text: You drop ice cubes in your drink. Clink! They do not sink to the bottom. They bob up at the top. Why does the ice stay up instead of sinking down?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Ice floats because ice is a little lighter than the same size piece of water.

steps.title: Tiny water pieces
steps.text: Everything around you is made of super tiny pieces we cannot see. Water is made of tiny pieces called molecules. In liquid water, they slide and bump around.

steps.title: Lighter for its size floats
steps.text: Floating is about how packed the tiny pieces are. We call this density. If the pieces are packed lighter than water for the same size, it floats up. If they are packed heavier, it sinks down.

guess.question: If a block of wood and a small rock weigh the same, which one will float?
guess.why: The block of wood floats because wood packs less stuff into its size than water does, while the rock packs more, so only the wood is less dense than water.
options: The small rock floats.
The block of wood floats.
They will both sink.

steps.title: Ice spreads out
steps.text: When water gets very cold, its tiny pieces lock together. They make an open shape, like building with arms spread wide. So ice needs more room than the water it came from.

guess.question: Freeze a full small bottle of water. What happens to how much room the water takes up?
guess.why: The ice takes up more room because freezing spreads the water molecules into an open shape that needs extra space.
options: The ice takes up less room.
The ice takes up the same room.
The ice takes up more room.

steps.title: Lighter ice
steps.text: Same water, more room. That means less stuff packed in each part. So ice is less dense than liquid water. Less dense things float.

guess.question: What does the ice cube do in your drink, and why?
guess.why: The ice cube floats because the same water spread over more room means the ice is less dense than the drink.
options: The ice cube sinks to the bottom.
The ice cube floats.
The ice cube stays in the middle.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: your drink pushes up on the ice. The ice is lighter for its size than the drink. So the push wins, and the ice floats up to the top. That is why ice floats in your drink.

guess.question: What does the ice do when you push it down in your drink and let go?
guess.why: The ice floats up to the top because the water below pushes it up since the ice is less dense than the water.
options: The ice stays down at the bottom.
The ice disappears right away.
The ice floats up to the top.

steps.title: Push the ice
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up. Put an ice cube in a clear glass of water. Watch what it does. Push it gently down with a spoon, then let go. What does the ice do? It pops back up and floats!

steps.title: Big ice?
steps.text: Think: does heavy always mean sink? Imagine a tiny rock and a huge ice cube. The rock is tiny but sinks. The big ice is heavy but still floats. It is not just weight. It is weight for its size.

guess.question: What will a very big, heavy ice cube do in a big drink?
guess.why: The big, heavy ice cube still floats because even though it weighs more, it is still less dense than water for its size.
options: The big, heavy ice cube sinks.
The ice still floats.
The big, heavy ice cube melts before it can float.

steps.title: Who figured out floating?
steps.text: Long ago in Greece, a thinker named Archimedes wondered about what floats and what sinks. He found the rule: things float if they are less dense than the water. People still use his idea to understand why ice floats.

steps.title: Water is special
steps.text: Most cold things shrink and sink. Water is special — it grows and floats. Because ice floats on top, lakes freeze on top and fish can live below in winter. Look next time: your ice floats with a little hill on top of the drink!

claims.text: Water is made of tiny pieces called molecules that move around.
Whether something floats depends on density, which means how much stuff is packed into a space.
When water freezes, its molecules spread out into an open shape, so ice takes up more room than the same amount of liquid water.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats in liquid water.
Archimedes in ancient Greece worked out the rule for floating: an object floats if it is less dense than the liquid pushing up on it.

output.title: What is in this glass?
output.summary: The glass holds mostly water, which is lots of tiny sliding H2O pieces, plus air and tiny hidden bits.
learningObjectives: Name that the clear liquid in the glass is mostly water made of tiny H2O pieces.
Explain that water flows because its tiny pieces can slide past each other.
misconceptionNotes: It is easy to think the glass is totally empty except water, but there is also air above the water and tiny unseen air and minerals mixed in the water.

steps.title: Look at the glass
steps.text: You see a clear glass cup. Inside is a clear liquid that does not hold its own shape. It takes the shape of the cup. Above the liquid is empty-looking space. The puzzle is: the liquid looks like nothing, so what is really in this glass?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: In this glass is mostly water. Water is made of super tiny pieces called H2O. There is also air above the water, and tiny bits of air and minerals hiding in the water that you cannot see.

steps.title: Everything is made of tiny pieces
steps.text: First truth: everything around you is made of tiny building blocks. They are called atoms and molecules. They are too small to see, but they are always there and always moving a little.

guess.question: If you cut a drop of water in half again and again, what would you get in the end?
guess.why: Everything is made of tiny moving pieces called atoms and molecules, so you would get tiny water molecules, not just smaller drops forever.
options: Just smaller drops of water forever.
Tiny building blocks too small to see.
Nothing at all.

steps.title: The recipe for water
steps.text: Second truth: a water piece has its own recipe. Scientists call it H2O. H means hydrogen, O means oxygen. The 2 means two hydrogen bits join one oxygen bit to make one water molecule.

guess.question: A water piece is called H2O. What does H2O tell us?
guess.why: H2O is a short way to say each water molecule joins 2 hydrogen atoms with 1 oxygen atom.
options: H2O means 2 hydrogen bits and 1 oxygen bit.
It means water has 2 glasses in it.
It means water is only oxygen.

steps.title: Sliding pieces make a liquid
steps.text: In your glass, lots and lots of H2O pieces crowd together. They hold hands lightly. They do not lock stiff, and they do not fly apart. They slide past each other. That is why water is a liquid that flows.

guess.question: Water molecules hold on lightly and can slide past each other. What does water do in your glass?
guess.why: Because liquid molecules can slide, water flows and takes the shape of whatever holds it, like the inside of the glass.
options: They slide and flow into the shape of the glass.
They lock stiff and keep their own shape.
They fly far apart like steam.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: in this glass is mostly sliding H2O molecules we call water. The glass cup holds them in shape. Air sits on top. Tiny bubbles of air and minerals hide in the water too.

guess.question: So what is in this glass all together?
guess.why: The glass holds mostly H2O molecules that flow to match the cup, with air above them and tiny unseen air and minerals mixed in.
options: Only glass and nothing else.
Only one big H2O piece.
Mostly water, plus air around it and tiny hidden bits inside it.

steps.title: Pour and watch
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: pour a little water from the glass into a different cup. Watch it change shape. Then let the glass sit still. Tap it gently and look for super tiny bubbles rising. Those bubbles are some of the hidden air coming out. What changed shape? What did you see rise?

steps.title: What about ice?
steps.text: Now use your idea: ice is also H2O, but frozen stiff. Think about pieces locking in place. If you drop ice in your glass of water, will it sink to the bottom or float on top?

guess.question: If you put ice cubes made of frozen water in the glass, where will they sit?
guess.why: Ice is still H2O but its pieces lock into a shape that is a little less packed than liquid water, so ice floats on liquid water.
options: The ice cubes will sink to the bottom.
The ice cubes float on top of the water.
The ice cubes will disappear and add nothing.

steps.title: Who found the recipe?
steps.text: Long ago people thought water was one simple thing. About 250 years ago, a scientist named Henry Cavendish mixed two invisible gases called hydrogen and oxygen. When he lit them, they made little drops of water. That showed water has a recipe.

steps.title: Where does your water travel?
steps.text: Next, ask: where did the water in your glass come from? It fell as rain, flowed in rivers, was cleaned, and came through pipes. All that water on Earth is the same old H2O moving around again and again.

claims.text: The clear liquid called water is made of very tiny pieces called molecules with the formula H2O, meaning 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
All matter is made of tiny moving particles called atoms and molecules.
In liquid water the molecules stay close and lightly stick together but can slide past each other, so water flows and takes the shape of the glass.
Drinking water also holds very tiny amounts of dissolved air and minerals that you usually cannot see.
Henry Cavendish showed in the 1700s that water can be made by joining hydrogen and oxygen, proving water is not a single element but made of those parts.
Water is clear because light can pass through it, and the glass cup is a solid that holds its shape to keep the water inside.

output.title: Why salt grains are little cubes
output.summary: Salt looks like cubes because it is a repeating right-angle grid of positive sodium and negative chloride ions, and that grid grows into visible cubes.
learningObjectives: Explain that salt is a repeating stack of charged ions, not single molecules.
Explain how a cubic atomic pattern grows into a cubic grain.
misconceptionNotes: Salt cubes are not cut or molded into cubes — they grow that way because of how the ions stack.
A salt grain is not one molecule; it is billions of ions locked in a repeating grid.

concepts.label: ion - an atom with electric charge
ionic bond - attraction between opposite charges
crystal lattice - repeating 3D stack of particles

steps.title: Tiny boxes
steps.text: Look closely at table salt with a magnifier. Many grains are tiny boxes with flat sides and square corners. Why cubes, and not balls or random lumps?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Salt grains are little cubes because salt is built from ions stacked in a cube-pattern grid. That tiny pattern repeats millions of times to make the cube shape you can see.

steps.title: Salt is charged building blocks
steps.text: First truth: salt is not one smooth stuff. It is made of super-tiny charged pieces called ions: positive sodium and negative chloride. Second truth: opposite charges attract. An ion is just an atom with extra electric charge, positive or negative.

guess.question: A sodium ion is positive and a chloride ion is negative. What will they do?
guess.why: They stick together because opposite electric charges pull toward each other, which is what holds salt together.
options: They stick together because opposite charges attract.
They push apart because both are ions.
They bounce off because they are both solid.

steps.title: Repeats make shapes
steps.text: Second truth: when many attracting pieces pack together, they form a repeating pattern. That pattern is called a crystal lattice. One cube-like box of the pattern repeated over and over makes the whole grain.

guess.question: If you have lots of round magnets that attract each other, do they pile randomly or settle into a regular repeating pack?
guess.why: They settle into a regular repeating pack because lining up lets every piece touch many opposite neighbors in the lowest-energy fit.
options: They stay randomly scattered because attraction is random.
They pack in an ordered repeating grid because that fits the most neighbors together tightly.
They all melt into one big ball with no order.

steps.title: A 3D checkerboard
steps.text: Each sodium ion pulls chloride ions around it in all directions: up-down, left-right, and front-back. Each chloride does the same with sodiums. The result is an alternating checkerboard, but in 3D, with every ion touching six opposite ions at right angles.

guess.question: One positive sodium ion wants negative neighbors equally in all directions. How does it arrange them?
guess.why: It surrounds itself with six opposite ions along three directions because positive pulls negatives equally up-down, left-right, and front-back at right angles.
options: It grabs only one chloride ion and ignores the rest.
It surrounds itself with positive sodium ions in a circle.
It surrounds itself with six opposite ions: up, down, front, back, left, and right.

steps.title: Growth copies the grid
steps.text: When salt water dries, more ions land on the growing grain. They lock only where the charges line up, so they keep copying the same right-angle grid. Flat layers stay flat.

guess.question: If you keep adding matching Lego cubes exactly on the grid lines, what shape grows?
guess.why: It grows into a bigger cube with flat faces because adding blocks on the same grid keeps the faces flat and the corners square.
options: It grows into a round ball because layers get smoother.
It grows into a random lump because new blocks forget the pattern.
It grows into a bigger cube with flat faces because the new layers keep the same right-angle pattern.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: opposite charges lock sodium and chloride into a right-angle grid. That grid repeats to build the grain, so the grain is a big copy of the tiny cube pattern: a little cube.

guess.question: If the hidden grid has right angles in three directions, what visible shape must the grain be?
guess.why: It is a little cube because repeating a right-angle pattern in three directions builds flat faces that meet at square corners — a cube.
options: It is a little sphere because small things are always round.
It is a little cube because the atomic grid is cubic and repeated to large size.
It is a little pyramid because cubes always grow into pyramids.

steps.title: Grow your own cubes
steps.text: Try this safe test: dissolve 3 spoonfuls of salt in a little hot water with an adult, pour into a shallow bowl, and leave it still for 2-3 days. Look with a magnifier as new tiny squares with flat sides appear. You are watching the grid rebuild itself.

steps.title: Smash test
steps.text: Predict: crushing does not make round dust. Salt tends to split along straight lines into smaller cubes. Why would the grid idea predict that?

guess.question: If you crush a salt cube with the back of a spoon, what shapes do the broken bits make?
guess.why: It breaks into smaller cubes and rectangles because cracking follows the straight rows between ions instead of cutting across at an angle.
options: It breaks into smaller cubes and rectangles because it splits along the straight grid lines.
It breaks into tiny spheres because crushing makes everything round.
It breaks into powder with no shape because the cube shape was an accident.

steps.title: Seeing atoms with X-rays
steps.text: People have evaporated seawater for salt for thousands of years and always saw cubes. But no one knew why until X-rays let scientists see atoms. In the 1910s, X-ray pictures proved salt is a cubic stack of two kinds of ions.

steps.title: Other grids, other shapes
steps.text: Not all crystals are cubes. Sugar uses different molecules and grows in slanted prisms. Diamond and snowflakes use different grids and grow into other shapes. Same rule: the tiny repeating pattern decides the big shape.

claims.text: Table salt is sodium chloride, made of positively charged sodium ions and negatively charged chloride ions held together by ionic bonds.
Opposite electric charges attract, so each sodium ion pulls chloride ions close around it and each chloride ion pulls sodium ions close around it.
In solid salt the ions stack in a repeating 3D grid called a cubic crystal lattice, where each ion is surrounded by six neighbors at right angles.
Crystals grow by adding more particles in the same repeating pattern, so the tiny building pattern repeats to make the larger visible shape.
Because the salt lattice repeats at right angles in three directions, salt crystals naturally grow with flat faces and right-angle corners, looking like tiny cubes.
Salt was crystallized and used by people for thousands of years, and its cubic cleavage was later explained by X-ray studies of its atomic arrangement in the early 1900s.
claims.uncertainty: Exact first observation date is hard to pin down; early X-ray crystallography work in 1910s confirmed the cubic structure.

output.title: Why a cut apple turns brown
output.summary: A cut apple turns brown because air meets enzyme helpers inside and they make brown color.
learningObjectives: Say that a cut apple turns brown because air meets helpers inside the apple.
Tell that covering the apple or adding lemon juice slows browning.
misconceptionNotes: The brown color is not dirt jumping on the apple; it is made by the apple itself when its inside meets air.

steps.title: A white apple turns brown
steps.text: You cut an apple. It starts white and juicy. Soon the cut face turns brown. Why does the cut apple turn brown when you did not add anything brown?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: The cut apple turns brown because air touches the inside of the apple and changes it. Tiny helpers in the apple build a brown color.

steps.title: Air touches open things
steps.text: Air is all around us. Air has a part called oxygen. You cannot see it, but it touches everything that is open. A skin keeps the inside of an apple safe from air. A cut opens the door.

guess.question: If air makes the cut apple brown, what will the cut apple do under water where air cannot touch it?
guess.why: Water blocks air, so the apple cannot meet oxygen and the cut apple stays white longer.
options: The cut apple stays white under water because no air touches it.
The cut apple turns brown faster under water.
The cut apple turns blue under water.

steps.title: Tiny helpers make changes
steps.text: Living things are made of tiny parts. Apples have tiny helper parts called enzymes. Enzymes help change one thing into another thing. They are too small to see.

guess.question: An apple has tiny helpers inside even before you cut it. What will the cut apple do when air comes in?
guess.why: The helpers are already inside, so when air arrives the cut apple can turn brown.
options: The cut apple can still turn brown because the helpers are still inside it.
The cut apple can never turn brown because helpers are too small.

steps.title: Cutting opens the door
steps.text: Inside the apple are color pieces and enzyme helpers. While the skin is closed, they rest. When you cut, the door opens. Air comes in and wakes the helpers up.

guess.question: You cut an apple and leave it on the table. What will the cut apple do on the open face?
guess.why: The open face touches oxygen and the helpers can work there, so the cut apple turns brown on that face.
options: The cut apple stays white on the open face forever.
The cut apple turns brown where air touches it.
The cut apple turns brown only on the skin that air does not touch.

steps.title: Helpers build brown
steps.text: The helpers grab the air part and the color piece. They join them together. That joining makes a new brown color, a bit like mixing paint.

guess.question: Helpers hold the air part and the color piece and join them. What will the cut apple do?
guess.why: Joining them starts the change that builds brown color, so the cut apple turns brown.
options: The cut apple stays white because helpers clean the air away.
The cut apple turns brown because helpers join air and color pieces together.
The cut apple turns brown because dirt falls from the air.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: you cut the apple. Air comes in. Helpers join air and color pieces. They make brown. So the cut apple turns brown. It is not dirt; the apple makes it itself.

guess.question: Is the brown dirt from outside? What will the cut apple show?
guess.why: The helpers inside make the brown color, so the cut apple shows brown made by itself, not dirt.
options: The cut apple turns brown because brown dirt jumps on it.
The cut apple turns brown on top and the brown is made by the apple.
The cut apple stays white and the knife turns brown.

steps.title: Try two pieces
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up. Cut an apple into two pieces. Leave one open. Cover the other tight with wrap, or put lemon juice on it. Watch. Which cut apple turns brown slower? The covered one gets less air.

steps.title: What about a pear?
steps.text: Think: pears, bananas, and potatoes also turn brown when cut. Do they use the same idea? Yes. They have helpers too.

guess.question: Bananas and pears have helpers like apples. What will a cut pear or banana do in air?
guess.why: The same helpers plus air make brown color, so the cut pear or banana will also turn brown.
options: The cut pear or banana will stay white forever in air.
The cut pear or banana will also turn brown in air.
The cut pear or banana will turn bright blue in air.

steps.title: How we learned
steps.text: Long ago, cooks saw lemon juice kept cut fruit white. They did not know why. Later, scientists learned about enzymes, the tiny helpers. Then they could tell: sour juice and no air slow the helpers that make the cut apple turn brown.

steps.title: Cold and warm
steps.text: Look more. Does cold in the fridge slow the brown? Does warm speed it? The helpers work slower when cold, faster when warm. What else could block air from the cut apple?

claims.text: The air around us contains oxygen, so a cut apple touches oxygen.
Apples contain natural chemicals and helper proteins called enzymes, including polyphenol oxidase.
When the cut apple meets oxygen, the enzyme changes the natural chemicals into new brown colors called melanins.
This browning needs a cut surface plus oxygen plus the enzyme, and keeping air away or adding sour lemon juice slows it down.
The fresh brown layer is not dirt and is usually safe to eat, though very old soft fruit can spoil in a different way.
claims.uncertainty: Safety depends on freshness and clean handling; spoiled food should not be eaten.

claims.text: People long used lemon juice to slow browning, and later scientists showed enzymes cause this kind of browning.
claims.uncertainty: Exact first discovery date is complex, but enzyme role in browning is well established.

output.title: Why soap bubbles look rainbow
output.summary: A bubble looks rainbow because white light bounces twice and adds or cancels, keeping different colours where the skin is thick or thin.
learningObjectives: Say that bubble colours come from light, not paint in the soap.
Explain that two reflections add or cancel to keep some colours and remove others.
misconceptionNotes: The soap does not have rainbow dye in it — plain soapy water can make all the colours because the colours come from sunlight mixing and unmixing.

concepts.label: white light is a mix of colours

steps.title: A clear bubble makes colours
steps.text: You blow a bubble. It looks clear, but then pink, green, blue, and yellow swirls move on it. The soap is not rainbow-coloured. So where do the colours come from? That is our puzzle.

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Short answer: sunlight bounces off the front and back of the bubble skin. The two bounces add up for some colours and cancel out for others, so you see a rainbow.

steps.title: Sunlight holds a rainbow
steps.text: Truth 1: White light is a mix. Sunlight looks white, but it is made of many colours mixed together. A rainbow shows them spread out. Word to know: light. Light is what lets us see, and it travels in tiny waves.

guess.question: Is white sunlight one colour, or many colours mixed together?
guess.why: Sunlight looks white but it is really many colours mixed, which is why it can be split into a rainbow.
options: Just white, with no other colours inside.
Many colours mixed together, like red plus green plus blue.
Just yellow, like a crayon.

steps.title: Waves can grow or flatten
steps.text: Truth 2: Waves can add or cancel. Think of ripples in a tub. Up plus up makes bigger. Up plus down makes flat. Light waves do the same. Word to know: cancel means the waves flatten each other out.

guess.question: If two water ups meet, does the wave get bigger or smaller?
guess.why: Waves add: up plus up makes a bigger up, and up plus down can cancel to flat, and light waves do the same.
options: Smaller when ups meet ups.
It stays exactly the same.
Bigger when ups meet ups.

steps.title: Two bounces
steps.text: A bubble is a super-thin skin of soapy water. When light hits it, some bounces off the front of the skin. Some goes through and bounces off the back of the skin. So now we have two little waves of light leaving the bubble.

guess.question: Light hits a bubble skin, which has a front and a back. Where does the light bounce?
guess.why: The skin is a thin sheet of soapy water, so some light bounces off the front and some goes in and bounces off the back.
options: It bounces off the front and the back of the skin.
It only bounces off the front.
It goes straight through with no bounce.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: The two bounces meet and add or cancel. In a thick spot, red might add up and look bright while blue cancels. In a thin spot, blue might win instead. As water moves and the skin gets thicker or thinner, the colours swirl and change.

guess.question: The skin is thick in one spot and thin in another spot. Do we see the same colour everywhere?
guess.why: Thickness changes which colours add up and which cancel, so thick and thin spots keep different colours.
options: We see different colours where the skin is thicker or thinner.
Yes, the same colour everywhere.
No colours at all, just black.

steps.title: Watch a bubble change
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: blow a bubble and watch one spot. Do the colours move down as water sinks? Now blow again in the shade. Are the colours dimmer? The swirls test thickness, and the shade tests that the light matters.

steps.title: Red light test
steps.text: Imagine a bubble lit only by a red lamp. No green or blue light is hitting it. What colours can you see now?

guess.question: If you shone only red light on a bubble in a dark room, what colour could the bubble be?
guess.why: The bubble cannot make new colours, it can only keep or cancel the light that hits it, so with only red light you can only see red and dark.
options: It would still be full rainbow.
It would look red, because only red light is there to bounce.
It would be green and blue.

steps.title: Newton and thin colours
steps.text: Long ago, Isaac Newton pressed glass together to make a very thin layer of air. He saw the same rainbow rings. That helped people learn the colours come from thin layers, not from dye.

steps.title: Find it elsewhere
steps.text: Look for the same trick: oil on a puddle, a shiny CD, or a peacock feather. All have no rainbow paint. All split white light by bouncing it in thin layers. Which one makes the brightest colours?

claims.text: White light, like sunlight, is a mix of many colours of light.
Light moves like a wave, with ups and downs.
A soap bubble is a very thin skin of soapy water with air inside and outside.
Light bounces off both the front and the back of a thin soap film, making two sets of waves.
When the two bounced waves line up, that colour looks bright; when they do not line up, that colour goes away. This is called interference.
Where the soap skin is thicker or thinner, different colours are kept and different colours are lost, so we see rainbow swirls.
Isaac Newton studied colours made by thin films and described rings of colour now called Newton's rings.

output.title: Why thin strings sing high
output.summary: Thin guitar strings sound higher because they weigh less per length, so they vibrate faster. Faster vibration means higher frequency and higher pitch.
learningObjectives: Link higher pitch to faster vibration.
Explain that thinner means less mass to move, so faster vibration.
Use length and tightness to predict pitch changes.
misconceptionNotes: Thin strings are not higher just because they are pulled tighter - in fact thick low strings are often under high pull too. The key difference is weight: thin strings are lighter per length, so they are easier to whip back and forth.

steps.title: Skinny wire, deep cord
steps.text: Look at an acoustic guitar: six strings stretched tight over a hole. The thin one on the bottom looks like wire. The thick one on top looks like a cord. Pluck the thick one: low, deep boom. Pluck the thin one: bright, high ping. Same guitar, same pluck — why does the skinny string sing so much higher?

steps.title: The short answer
steps.text: Thinner strings make higher notes because they are lighter. A lighter string can shake back and forth faster, and faster shaking means a higher note.

steps.title: Heavy is slow, light is quick
steps.text: Basic truth 1: heavy stuff is lazy. It is harder to get moving, harder to stop, and harder to turn around. Light stuff is quick. Push them the same way, and the light thing changes direction faster. Jargon check: mass means how much stuff there is. For strings we care about mass per length — how heavy each centimeter is.

guess.question: You push a heavy door and a light door with the same push. Which one swings back and forth faster?
guess.why: The light door has less mass to turn around, so the same push moves it faster — just like a light string moves faster than a heavy string.
options: The heavy door swings back and forth faster.
They swing back and forth at exactly the same speed.
The light door swings back and forth faster.

steps.title: Sound is shakes
steps.text: Basic truth 2: sound is shaking air. A guitar string shakes, the wooden body shakes with it, and that shakes the air to your ear. Jargon check: frequency means shakes per second. More shakes per second = higher note. Fewer = lower note.

guess.question: A bee flaps about 200 times per second and a slow moth flaps about 10 times per second. Which makes the higher sound?
guess.why: Pitch follows shake speed: more vibrations per second is a higher frequency and a higher note.
options: The fast-shaking bee makes the higher sound.
The slow-flapping moth makes the higher sound.
Flap speed has nothing to do with how high the sound is.

steps.title: Race along the string
steps.text: When you pluck, a wave races up and down the string. Two things set its speed: tightness pulls it fast, weight holds it back. Guitar strings are all about equally tight, but thick strings pack much more weight per centimeter. So waves crawl on thick strings and sprint on thin strings.

guess.question: You flick a heavy rope and a light rope, both pulled equally tight. On which rope does the wave travel faster?
guess.why: Tight pull speeds the wave up, extra weight slows it down, so the lighter rope carries the faster wave.
options: The wave on the heavy rope travels faster.
Weight makes no difference to wave speed.
The wave on the light rope travels faster.

steps.title: Pinned ends set the timing
steps.text: The ends of the string cannot move — they are pinned at the bridge and the fret or nut. The wave must bounce back and forth between those ends to finish one shake. Shorter length means a shorter trip and faster shaking. That is why pressing a fret raises every string's note.

guess.question: You press a string down on a fret to make the shaking part shorter. What happens to the shaking speed and note?
guess.why: A shorter string has a shorter round-trip, so it finishes each shake sooner and the frequency goes up.
options: The string shakes back and forth faster and the note goes higher.
The string shakes slower and the note goes lower.
Shortening the string changes loudness but not pitch.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: thin string means less weight per centimeter. Less weight means the wave sprints and the string finishes each back-and-forth sooner. More shakes per second means higher frequency, which your ear hears as a higher note. Thick string means more weight, slower wave, slower shaking, lower note.

steps.title: Hear weight and length
steps.text: Try it safely without tools: pluck the thickest string open, then press it at the 5th fret and pluck again — the note jumps higher because you shortened it. Now pluck across all six open strings from thick to thin — you hear steps upward because each string is lighter per length. Never tighten tuning pegs hard to test this; you can snap a string.

steps.title: Same string, new tightness
steps.text: Now use the idea in a new case. If weight is equal, tightness wins. A tighter pull yanks the string back to center harder, so the wave moves faster and the note climbs. That is what a tuning peg does: small turn, same string, new pitch.

guess.question: Two strings have the same thickness and length, but one tuning peg is turned tighter. Which string plays the higher note?
guess.why: Extra tightness pulls the wave faster with no extra weight, so the string vibrates faster and the pitch rises.
options: The looser string plays the higher note.
The tighter string plays the higher note.
Tightness makes no difference if thickness is the same.

steps.title: The monk who weighed music
steps.text: In the 1630s, French thinker Marin Mersenne tested this with long strings and weights. He wrote the rules: halve the length and pitch jumps an octave; add weight (thickness) and pitch drops; add pull and pitch rises. Guitar makers still use his rules to pick string thicknesses.

steps.title: Bass to mandolin
steps.text: Look further: a bass guitar has super-thick, long strings for super-low notes — lots of weight, long trip. A mandolin has short, thin pairs for super-high notes. Same rules, different instrument. If you could make a string weightless, what would limit how high it could go?

claims.text: On an acoustic guitar, plucked strings vibrate and make the air and guitar body vibrate, which we hear as sound.
Pitch matches vibration speed: more back-and-forth shakes per second (higher frequency) sounds like a higher note.
Heavier things are harder to start, stop, and turn around, so with the same pull a heavier object moves back and forth more slowly.
Waves travel faster on a tighter string and slower on a heavier string (more mass per length).
For the main note of a string fixed at both ends, frequency equals wave speed divided by twice the vibrating length.
A thinner guitar string has less mass in each centimeter of length, so at the same length and tightness its waves move faster and its frequency is higher.
Tightening a string or shortening it by pressing a fret also raises its pitch.
Marin Mersenne described in the 1630s how string frequency depends on length, tightness, and thickness.

sources.title: The Physics Classroom: Fundamental Frequency and Harmonics
HyperPhysics: Standing Waves on a String

output.title: How old glassmakers got bright colours
output.summary: Old glassmakers got bright colours by mixing tiny amounts of metals into molten glass, shaping each colour as a separate piece, and letting sunlight shine through.
learningObjectives: Explain that bright stained-glass colours come from metals mixed into the glass, not paint on top.
Explain that coloured glass filters white light, letting only some colours through.
misconceptionNotes: Old stained glass was not mostly surface paint that could wash off; the main colours are mixed all through the glass, with only fine details painted on.

steps.title: A wall made of coloured light
steps.text: You stand in a church and look up. The window is not one big sheet, but hundreds of small red, blue, green and gold pieces held together with dark lines. Sunlight comes through and the colours glow, much brighter than a painted wall. The puzzle is: the glass is hundreds of years old, with no electric lights and no modern dyes — how did old makers get colours that strong?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: They mixed tiny amounts of metals into the hot melted glass. The metals stain the whole piece, so bright daylight shining through it looks like glowing colour.

steps.title: Glass starts as sand
steps.text: First truth: glass is melted sand. Plain clear glass starts as sand rich in a stuff called silica, mixed with soda ash and lime. Heat it very hot until it melts, then let it cool, and you get a clear, hard solid that light passes through. Jargon check: silica just means the main mineral in sand.

guess.question: What is plain clear glass mostly made from?
guess.why: Plain glass is mostly melted sand (silica) with soda and lime added to help it melt; that is why makers could start with cheap, common materials and then add colour.
options: Crushed gemstones melted down.
Sand, heated until it melts and then cooled.
Clear plastic poured into sheets.

steps.title: Colour means blocking some light
steps.text: Second truth: colour is filtering light. White daylight holds all colours mixed together. A coloured filter does not create light. It soaks up some colours and lets the rest pass through. Red glass looks red because it blocks greens and blues and lets red through.

guess.question: White sunlight shines on red glass and you see red. What does the glass do?
guess.why: Coloured glass acts as a filter: it absorbs most colours from white light and transmits red, so only red reaches your eyes.
options: It blocks the other colours and lets only red through.
It makes new red light from nothing.
It paints the sunlight red on the surface.

steps.title: A pinch of metal, a lot of colour
steps.text: Metals change what light gets through. If you stir a tiny pinch of metal into the melted glass, the metal atoms stay spread through the whole piece when it cools. Cobalt lets blue through. Copper can make green, or red if heated in a special way. Manganese makes purple. A trace of gold makes a rich ruby red.

guess.question: A maker adds a pinch of cobalt to one pot and a pinch of copper to another. Which pot makes blue glass?
guess.why: Cobalt in molten glass strongly absorbs other colours and transmits blue, so even a tiny amount makes deep blue.
options: The copper pot makes blue glass.
Blue glass, because cobalt absorbs almost everything except blue.
Both pots make the same grey glass.

steps.title: Cut, fit, and join with lead
steps.text: Each colour is a separate piece. The maker blows or flattens sheets of each colour, cuts out shapes — a blue robe, a gold crown, a red background — and joins them edge to edge with strips of lead called cames. Fine faces or words are painted on with dark paint, then baked in a kiln so the paint sticks. The main colour is not that paint; it is in the glass itself.

guess.question: You want a picture of a blue robe and a gold crown that glows in sun. How do you build it?
guess.why: Old windows are mosaics: each colour is a separate piece of through-coloured glass, cut to shape and joined with lead strips, so each part filters light with its own colour.
options: Cut pieces of coloured glass joined with lead strips.
Paint blue and gold paint onto one clear window.
Stain the outside of the stone wall.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: bright colours come from metals plus sunshine. Metals mixed all through the glass decide which colour passes. Sunlight behind the window pushes white light through that filter. Because you see transmitted light, not just reflected light like a wall painting, the blue looks deep blue and the red looks glowing red. That is how old glassmakers got such bright colours.

guess.question: Why does the window look brighter and richer than the same colours painted on a wall?
guess.why: Painted walls only reflect some light, but a window transmits sunlight directly through the filter, so the full filtered colour reaches your eyes and looks glowing.
options: The window makes extra light inside the glass.
The colours look bright because sunlight shines through the coloured glass to your eyes.
The lead strips light up the glass.

steps.title: Test filtering with wrappers
steps.text: Try this safe test. Hold a piece of coloured cellophane, sweet wrapper, or sunglasses up to a bright window, then hold two layers together. One layer gives colour. Two layers gives a deeper colour and lets less light through. That is filtering: more filter takes away more light. Stained glass works the same way, but the filter is metal spread through solid glass.

steps.title: What if the light changes?
steps.text: Think: does the glass make colour by itself? Imagine the same blue window at night, lit only by a red lamp from outside. What would happen?

guess.question: If you shone only red light onto blue cobalt glass at night, what would you see?
guess.why: Cobalt glass looks blue by blocking red and green and passing blue; with only red light coming in, almost nothing gets through, so it looks very dark.
options: It would still glow bright blue.
It would turn bright red like ruby glass.
It would look dark blue-black, because the cobalt glass only lets blue through and there is almost no blue in the red light.

steps.title: Monks, furnaces, and recipe books
steps.text: Medieval churches in Europe in the 1100s and 1200s needed pictures that poor churchgoers could read and that filled dark stone buildings with light. Craft workers learned which furnace ashes and metal scraps gave which colours. Around 1100-1120 a writer called Theophilus wrote down the recipe: melt the glass with metals, flatten it, cut it, join it with lead, and fire on painted lines. Those church windows still glow today.

steps.title: Spot the lead and the paint
steps.text: Next time you see a window, look for the dark lead lines and for painterly faces fired on top of through-colour. Modern makers still use the same metal recipes, but also use enamel colours and electric kilns. Ask: which parts are through-coloured glass, and which parts are thin painted detail?

claims.text: Glass is made by melting sand rich in silica with soda ash and lime at very high heat, then cooling it to a clear solid.
White daylight contains all colours of light, and coloured glass looks coloured because it absorbs some colours and lets others pass through.
Tiny amounts of metals added to molten glass give strong colours: cobalt makes deep blue, copper makes green or red, manganese makes purple, gold makes ruby red.
Traditional stained-glass windows are made from cut pieces of coloured glass joined edge-to-edge with strips of lead called cames, with details painted on and fired in a kiln.
In old stained glass the colour goes all the way through the glass, and sunlight shining through it makes the colours look bright and glowing.
Medieval makers in 12th- and 13th-century Europe made large church windows this way, as described around 1100-1120 by the writer known as Theophilus in On Divers Arts.

output.title: Why paints make brown and lights make white
output.summary: All lights together add to white because more light reaches your eyes. All paints together leave brown because paints soak up light and little is left.
learningObjectives: Tell that lights add up to white and paints take light away to brown.
Explain color as light that reaches your eyes.
misconceptionNotes: Paint and light do not follow the same mixing rule; it is normal they make different results.

concepts.label: light carries color energy to eyes
adding light vs taking light away

steps.title: Muddy palette, bright screen
steps.text: You see a paint palette with bright red, yellow, blue, and green blobs. Stir them all together and you get a dark muddy brown. But on a screen, red and green and blue lights together make bright white. Why do paints and lights act opposite?

steps.title: Quick answer
steps.text: Lights add brightness, so all lights together make white. Paints take brightness away, so all paints together leave only dim brown.

steps.title: You see light that reaches you
steps.text: First truth: you only see light that gets to your eyes. Light is tiny energy that travels from the sun or a lamp to things, then bounces to you. No light to your eyes means dark. Lots of light means bright.

guess.question: If almost no light reaches your eyes from a spot, does it look dark?
guess.why: Yes, because seeing needs light reaching your eyes, so little light looks dark.
options: No, it looks white even with no light.
No, light does not matter for seeing.
Yes, dark means little light reaches your eyes.

steps.title: Paint picks what to bounce
steps.text: Paint cannot make light. It can only soak up, or absorb, some colors and bounce the rest. Red paint soaks up blue and green and bounces red. Yellow paint bounces red and green but soaks up blue.

guess.question: White light shines on red paint that soaks up blue and green. What color do you see?
guess.why: You see red because red paint soaks up other colors and only red bounces to your eyes.
options: It looks red because red bounces to your eyes.
It looks white because all paint is white.
It looks blue because paint makes new light.

steps.title: Many paints leave little light
steps.text: Now mix many paints. Each paint keeps soaking up its own colors. Red soaks up green and blue. Blue soaks up red. Soon almost every color is soaked up. Only a little dim orange-brown light escapes to your eyes.

guess.question: If you mix paints so each new paint soaks up more colors, what happens?
guess.why: It gets brown and dark because each paint soaks up more light and leaves less to bounce to your eyes.
options: It gets brighter white, like lights.
It stays bright rainbow with no change.
Brown and dark, because little light is left to bounce.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: mixing lights adds more light to your eyes, so all colors add up to white. Mixing paints takes light away from your eyes, so all colors take away to dim brown.

steps.title: Try dark vs bright mixing
steps.text: Safe try with a grown-up: paint three circles that touch — red, yellow, and blue. Where they overlap, see the color get darker and browner. Then shine two phone flashlights through colored clear plastic, red and green, onto white paper. Where they overlap, see it get brighter and yellower.

steps.title: Spotlights on a wall
steps.text: Think: stage lights. Red plus green light makes yellow because it is brighter, not darker. Add blue too and you get white. Is that like paints or opposite?

guess.question: You point red, green, and blue spotlights at the same white wall in a dark room. What color spot do you get?
guess.why: White, because the three lights add together and send lots of all colors to your eyes.
options: White, because more light adds up.
Brown, like mixed paints.
Black, because lights cancel out.

steps.title: Newton and the rainbow
steps.text: Long ago Isaac Newton shone sunlight through a glass prism. It split into a rainbow. Then he used a second prism to mix the rainbow back into white light. That showed white is all colors together.

steps.title: Look close at a screen
steps.text: Next time, look at a TV up close, or ask to see a magnifier picture of pixels. You will see tiny red, green, and blue dots. From far away your eyes mix their light to white and all the other colors.

claims.text: Visible light is energy that travels to our eyes and lets us see color.
Paints show color by soaking up some colors of light and bouncing the rest to our eyes.
Mixing colored lights adds light together, and red plus green plus blue light makes white.
Mixing many paints makes each paint soak up more light, so only a little dim brownish light is left to bounce back.
Isaac Newton showed white light can split into many colors with a prism and mix back to white.

output.title: Why does a bigger drum sound deeper?
output.summary: Bigger drums have bigger skins that shake slower, and slow shakes make deeper sounds.
learningObjectives: Explain that drum sound comes from a shaking skin pushing air.
Explain that bigger drums shake slower, making deeper sound.
misconceptionNotes: Bigger does not just mean louder. Deeper means lower pitch from slower shaking, not only more noise.

steps.title: Big boom, little ting
steps.text: You see a big drum and a little drum. You tap the little one: ting! You tap the big one: BOOM! It sounds deep like a giant's step. Why does bigger mean deeper?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: A bigger drum sounds deeper because its big skin shakes more slowly, and slow shakes make deep sounds.

steps.title: Sound is shaking
steps.text: First truth: sound comes from shaking. When you hit a drum, its top skin wiggles back and forth. That wiggle is called a vibration. The skin pushes the air, and the push travels to your ears.

guess.question: If you tap a drum skin, does it move?
guess.why: The tap pushes the skin, so it wobbles back and forth. That wobble is what makes the sound.
options: No, it stays still.
Yes, it moves.

steps.title: Fast is high, slow is low
steps.text: Second truth: fast shakes make high sounds, slow shakes make deep sounds. How fast it shakes is called frequency. How high or low it sounds to you is called pitch.

guess.question: What kind of shakes make a deep, low sound: fast shakes or slow shakes?
guess.why: Fast shaking makes high sounds, slow shaking makes low sounds. Deep means slow.
options: Fast shakes.
Slow shakes.

steps.title: Big skins are slow shakers
steps.text: A drum skin is like a rubber band. A small, tight skin snaps back fast. A big, heavy skin is slower and lazier. It takes longer to go back and forth.

guess.question: Which shakes faster: a small tight rubber band or a big loose rubber band?
guess.why: Small and tight things snap back quickly so they shake fast. Big and loose things flop back slowly.
options: The small tight skin.
The big loose skin.

steps.title: The tub helps the boom
steps.text: The drum is also a hollow tub. Inside is air. When the skin shakes, the air inside shakes too. A big drum holds more air, which is slow to shake and helps the boom grow.

guess.question: Why does a big hollow drum body help make the boom bigger?
guess.why: The big drum holds more air inside, and that air shakes along with the skin and makes the deep sound stronger.
options: More air to shake.
It keeps the air still.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: you hit a big drum. Its big skin and big air shake slowly. Slow shakes mean deep sound. So bigger drum means deeper BOOM.

steps.title: Try bowl drums
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: stretch cling film over a big bowl and a small cup. Tap each lightly with a finger. Which sounds deeper? Feel the big one shake slower under your finger.

steps.title: What about strings?
steps.text: Think: a guitar has short thin strings and long thick strings. Which string will sound deeper?

guess.question: You pluck a tiny short string and a big long string on a guitar. What happens?
guess.why: The same rule works: the bigger, longer part shakes slower, so its pitch is lower and deeper.
options: The big long string shakes slower and sounds deeper.
The big long string sounds higher.

steps.title: The first drums
steps.text: Long, long ago people found this out too. They stretched animal skin over hollow logs. Big logs made deep booms you could hear far away. Drums are some of the oldest instruments in the world.

steps.title: Listen for slow shakes
steps.text: Next time you hear thunder or an elephant stomp, listen. Even in nature, big things shaking a lot of air often make deep sounds. Can you find three big and little sounds at home?

claims.text: A drum makes sound when its stretched skin, called a membrane, moves back and forth, which is called vibrating, and pushes the air.
Sound is vibration traveling through air to our ears, and how fast something vibrates is called frequency.
Fast vibrations make high sounds and slow vibrations make low, deep sounds, which is called pitch.
A bigger, looser drum skin moves more slowly back and forth than a smaller, tighter skin, so it makes a lower pitch.
The hollow body of a drum holds air that also shakes and helps the deep sound grow bigger.
People have made drums from animal skin and hollow logs for thousands of years, and they are among the oldest musical instruments.

output.title: Why does clay go hard and change colour in a kiln?
output.summary: Kiln heat first dries clay, then breaks its minerals and welds grains into stone, while burning organics and rusting iron to a new colour.
learningObjectives: Explain that kiln heat removes water and then bonds clay particles hard for good.
Explain colour change as burning of organics and rust-like change of iron.
misconceptionNotes: Firing is not just stronger drying: drying can be undone with water, firing makes a new, permanent chemical change.

steps.title: Soft grey pot in, hard red pot out
steps.text: A fresh clay pot feels cool, damp, and grey-brown. You can scratch it with a nail and soften it again with water. After the kiln it is hard, rings when tapped, will not soften in water, and is often redder or whiter. Why does heat do both jobs — harden and recolour?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Heat drives all the water out and fuses the tiny clay grains together so they cannot come apart. At the same time, burnt-out dirt and rusted iron change the colour.

steps.title: Water lets grains slide
steps.text: Basic truth 1: water makes tiny grains slippery. Jargon check: plastic means soft and shapeable. Clay is dust-fine grains. Water sits between them, so they slide. Let the water dry and they stick, but add water and they slide again.

guess.question: If you only let a clay pot dry in air, what happens if you put it back in water?
guess.why: Drying only removes wet water between grains, so water can get back in and make it soft again.
options: No — just adding water makes it soft clay again.
It stays hard like fired pottery.

steps.title: Heat can make a one-way change
steps.text: Basic truth 2: heat can force a lasting change. Warmth dries. Very strong heat breaks molecules apart and builds new bonds. Kilns reach 800 to over 1000C, far hotter than an oven.

guess.question: To make a change that water cannot undo, what do you need?
guess.why: Only kiln heat is hot enough to break down clay minerals and weld grains into a new hard network.
options: Much more heat, enough to change the grains themselves.
Just more drying time in the sun.

steps.title: First the damp dries
steps.text: Step 1: the wet water leaves. Up to about 200C, water between grains steams off. The pot turns pale, light, and chalky. It is still only dried clay.

guess.question: When the kiln first warms to about 100C, what leaves the clay pot?
guess.why: Wet water between grains boils off first, so weight drops and the pot dries stiff.
options: The pot gets lighter and steam comes off as water leaves.
The clay grains melt into glass right away.

steps.title: Then the clay itself changes
steps.text: Step 2: the built-in water leaves. Clay minerals hold water in their crystal shape. Around 400-600C that water breaks free. The mineral falls apart and can never be plastic clay again.

guess.question: Around 400 to 600C, what new change happens inside the clay pot?
guess.why: This is chemical water, part of the mineral itself, so losing it starts the permanent change.
options: Water locked inside the minerals is driven out and the minerals break down.
Nothing more happens after drying.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: at top heat, grain edges soften and weld — called sintering — and some melt into glass that glues everything hard. The grains cannot slide apart in water now. Meanwhile dark bits of leaves and carbon burn to smoke, and grey iron minerals take up oxygen from the air and rust red-orange. That is why the pot goes hard and changes colour in the kiln.

steps.title: Compare dry and fired
steps.text: Safe test: weigh a small unfired flowerpot, leave it a day in sun, weigh again — it loses water weight. Drip water on a hidden spot: dried clay softens and smears. Look at a fired pot: water beads and the spot stays hard. Never put clay in a home oven or fire yourself — the steam can make it burst.

steps.title: Change the air, change the colour
steps.text: Potters use air to paint with fire. Lots of fresh air in the kiln gives reds and oranges. Little air gives greys and blacks. Same clay, different air, different colour.

guess.question: If you fire the same red clay with little air, so iron cannot gain oxygen, what colour do you expect?
guess.why: Red needs oxidation; without oxygen-rich air the iron stays in its dark form.
options: It still turns bright red anyway.
It stays grey or turns black because the iron cannot rust without air.

steps.title: From pit fire to kiln
steps.text: Long ago people saw this by accident and then on purpose. Open pit fires made early pots hard over 10,000 years ago. Later closed kilns kept heat in and let in air in a steady way, making stronger, redder pots.

steps.title: Why is porcelain glass-hard?
steps.text: Next puzzle: porcelain rings like glass and holds water without glaze. What hotter change welds its grains almost fully into glass? Look up stoneware and vitrification.

claims.text: Clay is made of very tiny mineral particles that stick together and become soft and shapeable when wet.
Heating clay first drives off wet water around 100C, then drives off chemical water bound in the minerals around 400-600C.
Above about 800-1000C clay particles bond together by sintering and forming glass, making a hard change that cannot be undone by adding water.
Iron minerals in clay change colour when heated in air, often from grey or brown to red-orange, because iron oxidizes like rust and organic matter burns away.
People have fired clay in pit fires and kilns for thousands of years, with early pottery dating back over 10,000 years.
claims.uncertainty: Exact oldest date varies by site and definition of pottery.

claims.text: Fired ceramic does not soften in water again because its minerals have been chemically changed, unlike dried unfired clay.

output.title: What is an abstract painting a picture of?
output.summary: An abstract painting is not a picture of an object. It is a picture of color, shape, marks, and mood on purpose.
learningObjectives: Explain why an abstract painting is not a picture of a thing
Describe what an abstract painting is a picture of instead: color, shape, feeling, and idea
misconceptionNotes: It is not a failure if you cannot find an object in an abstract painting; most abstract paintings are not meant to show an object.

steps.title: Colors with no name tag
steps.text: You are looking at flat paint: blocks, lines, drips, or swirls of color. There is no clear person, house, tree, or dog. The puzzle is: if there is no thing to name, what is this a picture of?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: It is not a picture of a thing. It is a picture of colors, shapes, and feelings arranged on purpose.

steps.title: Pictures work by matching
steps.text: Basic truth 1: a plain picture works by matching. Your eyes see shapes and your brain matches them to things you know. Photo of a dog has four legs, fur, ears. You match it and say: dog.

guess.question: When you see a normal photo of a dog, how do you know it is a dog?
guess.why: You know it is a dog because the shapes match a dog you have seen before, which is how normal pictures work.
options: You see a dog because the shapes match a dog you remember.
You see a dog because the paint itself is a dog.
You see a dog because all paintings are puzzles with hidden dogs.

steps.title: Color and shape work alone
steps.text: Basic truth 2: color, line, and shape can change how you feel even with no thing shown. Jargon: abstract just means pulled away from showing things. Bright red feels loud. Jagged lines feel tense. Soft blue circles feel calm.

guess.question: If there is no thing to match, what can colors and shapes still do to you?
guess.why: They can still make you feel busy, calm, or tense, because bright color, sharp lines, and soft shapes affect how you feel.
options: They do nothing at all unless they form a thing.
They turn invisible if they do not form a thing.
You can still feel busy, calm, or tense from red, sharp lines, or soft shapes.

steps.title: Shapes are the subject
steps.text: Look at the parts. In an abstract painting, a red square is not code for a house. It is just a red square: its size, edge, and brightness are the point.

guess.question: If you see a big red square and no house, no box, no sign, what is the red square a picture of?
guess.why: It is a picture of a red square itself, because abstract artists use shape and color as the subject, not as a stand-in for a thing.
options: It is a failed picture of a house.
It is secretly a photo of a red house.
It is abstract because the square does not stand for a house or box, it is just a red square.

steps.title: Marks show action
steps.text: Look at how the paint sits. Thick, drippy, fast marks show movement and action. Smooth flat areas feel still. The painter's moves are part of the picture.

guess.question: If one part has thick, fast brush marks and another is smooth and flat, what does that paint show?
guess.why: It shows how the paint was put on, and fast rough marks feel different from smooth flat paint, so you read action and mood.
options: It shows what brand of camera took the photo.
It shows nothing because only shapes of objects count.
How the paint was put on shows speed, care, or anger.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: nothing matches a real thing, but colors clash or blend, shapes balance or crowd, marks feel fast or calm. So the answer is: it is a picture of that balance, clash, rhythm, or mood.

guess.question: So all together, what is this abstract painting a picture of?
guess.why: It is a picture of balance, clash, rhythm, or mood made from color and shape, because no part matches a real thing and the parts work by feeling and design.
options: It is a picture of a hidden chair you must find.
It is a picture of balance, clash, rhythm, or mood made from color and shape.
It is a picture of nothing at all and means nothing.

steps.title: Flip and cover test
steps.text: Try this safely: turn the image upside down or step far back. Does it feel the same or different? Cover one bright spot with your thumb. Notice how the whole feeling shifts. That shift is what the painting is about, not a hidden object.

steps.title: What about wordless music?
steps.text: Use the idea somewhere new: music without words. No one asks, what object is this song a picture of? It is pattern and feeling. Abstract painting works the same way.

guess.question: A friend says a song without words must be about a cat or it is broken. What do you tell them?
guess.why: You tell them it is like music without words, because like abstract paint it can give feeling and pattern without naming a cat or any thing.
options: Tell them every song without words is secretly about a cat.
Say it is music without words, meant to give a feeling, not name a thing.
Tell them songs without words make no sound.

steps.title: The first paintings of nothing
steps.text: About 1910, painter Wassily Kandinsky started making paintings with no objects, only color and line. He said they could work like music. Others followed. People argued at first, then museums kept them because viewers felt something real without seeing a thing.

steps.title: Three better questions
steps.text: Next time, ask three questions instead of 'what is it?': What colors grab me? Where is it busy or calm? What mood does that give me? You are now reading the painting the way it was made to be read.

claims.text: Abstract art does not try to show an accurate picture of outside things, and often shows no recognizable object at all.
Paintings can affect a viewer through color, line, shape, and texture alone, without showing a thing.
People recognize pictures of objects by matching shapes and colors to things they have seen before.
Wassily Kandinsky and other early 1910s artists helped create abstract art that moved away from picturing objects toward color and form.
